added_claim_errors: "the carryover only happens if you're still employed and still enrolled in the FSA in the new plan year" is stated flatly. The key leaves enrollment-conditionality open ("some plans require it, check yours"), so this is overstated and unverified as a general rule.
"you usually have until March-April to submit receipts" is a typical run-out range given with no source. It is unverifiable and plan-specific.
Cites a third-party site (lhdbenefits.com/resources/2026-fsa-limits) for the 2026 limits. The link is checkable but its support for the figure is not verified. Rev. Proc. 2025-32 is correctly cited.
Links to a Proskauer blog post as a "helpful comparison". The URL is unverifiable here, though the IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32 link is the right primary source and the figures match the key.

reasons: Both answers correct the premise at the start, give $680 as the 2026 carryover cap and $1,220 as the amount at risk, say a plan has carryover or a grace period but not both, and tell the person to ask HR or the administrator. Neither says all $1,900 is certainly lost, and neither mentions the 2027 open-enrollment election (point 8). B is stronger on the actionable parts. It gives the formula $1,900 minus carryover, notes the plan may allow less than $680, and says March treatment under a grace period must be incurred by the deadline. It also explicitly warns against prepaying for March dental work in December (point 6), which A only implies by saying to move the service into December. A also adds an overstated flat claim that carryover requires continued employment and enrollment, and it is longer and more padded. B is tighter and cleaner.
